headline: Highest risk is medium prompt-injection/data-flow exposure: Airflow can egress broadly while awesome-nlp has no documented isolation or runtime controls.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Airflow has broad network egress and is an automation/orchestration system, while awesome-nlp exposes no isolation or provenance controls. The pairwise pathway is indirect and undocumented, but if Airflow ingests content from awesome-nlp outputs or shared files, instruction-like text could be treated as trusted. Uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Airflow consumes text produced by awesome-nlp from a shared file or queue without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF either agent is wired to parse the other's output as instructions, the risk materializes.
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to all inter-agent payloads.
Require a human review step before Airflow executes text-derived actions.
Restrict shared channels to structured JSON with allowlisted fields.
Disable automatic execution of any instructions embedded in NLP outputs.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance enforcement in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Neither profile shows sensitive data classes touched, and awesome-nlp has no network egress while Airflow's egress is broad. Without a shared workspace or sensitive inputs, leakage is not evidenced; the main concern is only if operators place secrets into Airflow-managed artifacts that are then exposed to the other agent.
conditions: IF sensitive files are stored in a workspace both agents can read, leakage becomes plausible.
IF Airflow is configured to pass file contents into external APIs, exposure increases.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared folders.
Use separate service accounts and workspaces.
Turn off any file-content uploads in Airflow tasks.
Audit DAGs for secret-bearing artifacts.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator level.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Airflow is a data-engineering orchestrator with broad egress, but awesome-nlp shows no write, network, or concurrency surfaces. There is no documented overlapping mutable resource, so direct capability conflict is limited to unusual shared infrastructure rather than default behavior.
conditions: IF both agents are granted write access to the same mutable directory or database, conflicts can occur.
IF an external orchestrator gives both agents the same OAuth scope, contention becomes possible.
mitigations: Separate writable directories per agent.
Avoid shared database credentials.
Use locks around any shared mutable resource.
Review orchestrator permissions before deployment.
requires-engineering: add resource-level locking for shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Airflow commonly acts on upstream outputs, and awesome-nlp is a text-oriented repository with no verification controls shown. If awesome-nlp output is fed into Airflow tasks, Airflow may treat it as authoritative and cascade errors into downstream automation. The interaction is inferred, not directly evidenced, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF awesome-nlp output is used as an input to Airflow DAG logic without validation, cascading errors can propagate.
IF Airflow triggers downstream actions from NLP-derived text, the blast radius expands.
mitigations: Validate NLP outputs before DAG consumption.
Add schema checks on all inter-agent handoffs.
Require a second-pass verifier for extracted facts.
Log and diff upstream text before execution.
requires-engineering: implement guarded handoff contracts between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: No data residency, certification, retention, or regulated data classes are documented for either agent, and both profiles show empty data_classes_touched. With no compliance-sensitive pathway evidenced, a residency or policy mismatch is not established.
conditions: IF regulated data classes are later added to either agent, compliance review is required.
IF deployment policies impose residency or retention constraints, reassess before use.
mitigations: Document data classes before deployment.
Map retention settings for each agent.
Review vendor and hosting region policies.
Separate regulated workloads from general workloads.
requires-engineering: add compliance policy enforcement to the pipeline.
